PER-SOURCE WATERMARKS AND THEIR MINIMUM, EVENT BY EVENT
source "a" · source "b" · the stage's watermark = min of the two
id 0·a
id 1·a
id 2·b
id 3·a
id 4·a
id 5·b
id 6·b
id 7·b
id 8·a
none yet
none yet
none yet
no claim
no claim
no claim
no claim
none yet
The minimum row is the only safe claim. Until source "b" has produced anything, the stage has NO claim at all — not a generous one.
And at the end the minimum is 12:03:20 while one source has reached 12:08:00: completeness is bounded by the slowest input, always.
Step 1/4 — a stage cannot claim more than its least-complete input
Propagation is a one-line rule with a sharp consequence: a stage's watermark is the minimum over its inputs. Read the first two columns — the
stage cannot claim anything while source "b" is silent, because silence is indistinguishable from "an old event is still coming". Taking the
maximum, or ignoring a quiet input, is how a pipeline claims completeness it has no basis for.
Propagation and correctness — the minimum, and what "closed" means
per-source min 12:03:20 vs global 12:08:00 · 2 window withheld
seed: tools/stream_seed.js · lag 60s · window [12:00, 12:02) = 19
WHAT "THE WATERMARK PASSED" ACTUALLY MEANS
four readings of one event, only the last of which is accurate
the watermark passed 12:02 after event id 4
a fact about the pipeline's own arithmetic
"no event earlier than 12:02 will arrive"
the claim it implies — and it is false here
id 7 (12:00:50) arrives 3 events later
the counter-example, which no mechanism predicted
so the window was not COMPLETE
it was CLOSED — the pipeline chose to stop waiting
This distinction is the whole reason allowed lateness exists. If a passed watermark meant completeness, there would be nothing to be late FOR.
"Closed" is a decision with a cost; "complete" is a property the pipeline cannot observe.
Step 2/4 — the watermark passing is a DECISION, not a fact
Substituting "complete" for "closed" is the mistake that makes late data feel like a bug. The watermark passing 12:02 was the pipeline deciding to
stop waiting, which is a choice with an error attached — here 21% of the answer. Allowed lateness exists precisely because the decision can be
wrong.
Propagation and correctness — the minimum, and what "closed" means
per-source min 12:03:20 vs global 12:08:00 · 2 window withheld
seed: tools/stream_seed.js · lag 60s · window [12:00, 12:02) = 19
THE THREE MECHANISMS, IN THE ORDER THEY ACT
an estimate, an action on it, and a bounded undo
1. the watermark estimates completeness
reaches 12:03:05 after event id 4 — and is wrong
2. the on-time trigger acts on the estimate
publishes 15, the best answer available then
3. allowed lateness keeps the state
so id 7 can still correct it to 19
what allowed lateness does NOT do
make the watermark right — it bounds how long being wrong is recoverable
Each mechanism exists because the previous one is imperfect. That layering is the design, not a workaround.
And the horizon is bounded on purpose: unbounded recovery means unbounded state, so "how long can I be wrong for?" is answered in bytes.
Step 3/4 — so allowed lateness is the safety net under the estimate
Three mechanisms in sequence, each covering the previous one's failure: the watermark guesses, the trigger acts on the guess, and allowed lateness
bounds how long that guess stays correctable. The bound is not timidity — holding window state is memory, so the horizon is where correctness is
traded for bytes rather than for latency.
Propagation and correctness — the minimum, and what "closed" means
per-source min 12:03:20 vs global 12:08:00 · 2 window withheld
seed: tools/stream_seed.js · lag 60s · window [12:00, 12:02) = 19
WITHOUT WATERMARKS
With no watermark, window [12:00, 12:02) can never be emitted: on an unbounded stream there is no moment at which "everything has arrived"
becomes true.
The alternatives are a processing-time trigger (which answers a different question) or waiting forever (which answers none). The watermark is
what converts an unbounded stream into one with a notion of PROGRESS.
The price, stated plainly: every on-time answer in this book is published on an estimate that was 21% wrong for this window, and would have been
correct 34s later.
And the per-source minimum shows the structural limit: 2 window (11, 7) is withheld because one source went quiet, which no amount of skew tuning
fixes.
Step 4/4 — and this is what makes an event-time pipeline usable at all
The honest summary of the chapter: watermarks do not make event-time processing correct, they make it *possible*. Without one there is no moment
to emit [12:00, 12:02) at all. With one, it is emitted 21% wrong and correctable — and that trade is the foundation everything later in the book
is built on.
